title: Seat a resident's lower denture on her lower ridge
instruction: Put the care manikin's clean lower denture back in its mouth, seated on its lower gum, then take your hand away.
context: In nursing homes and hospitals, nursing assistants give residents mouth and denture care every morning and evening, and cleaning a denture and returning it to the resident is one of the skills on the nurse-aide competency exam (NNAAP). Nursing assistants (O*NET 31-1131.00) number about 1.4 million in the US. Putting a lower denture back in is the fiddly part. The denture is barely narrower than the open mouth, so it has to go in square and centred. Inside, it must come down back first onto the toothless ridge, its inner flanges either side of the tongue, with the soft lower lip pushed down out of the way. It is then let down at the front until its channel sits on the ridge all round. A lower denture left on the ridge's crest or cocked on one side rocks, rubs sores in the gum and falls out when the resident eats.
setup: Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them; heights are above the table. Two arms (bases 61 cm apart), one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. (1) A seated resident's head: a nursing-care training manikin with removable full dentures (a Kyoto Kagaku oral-care trainer, about $800), or the low-cost rig in the task's fixture folder, about $60 in materials. The rig is printed from STL files written from the task file's own geometry: the mouth in two halves, a riser, and a lower denture whose channel matches the printed ridge. Its lower lip is cast in Ecoflex 00-30 silicone in a printed mould and glued into a pocket in the chin. Build steps and checks are in the README. The head faces the arms on the centre line. Her lips' front is 35.5 cm forward and her open mouth is centred 20 cm up; the mouth opening is 6.6 cm wide and 4.9 cm high, and the lips are 1.2 cm thick. Her upper denture is in. The lower lip gives: about 2 N on its top edge pushes it down 1 cm. Behind it, the inside of the mouth is 7.6 cm wide. Her lower ridge (toothless gum) runs round in a U, 8 mm wide, its centre line 2 cm in radius with the arch's centre 5 cm behind the lips' front, its sides running 3.2 cm back from there. Its crest is 2.5 cm below the mouth's centre. Her tongue (2 cm wide) lies inside the U, just below the crest. (2) Her lower full denture: a horseshoe 6.1 cm across and 5 cm front to back, 2.1 cm tall, 25 g. It has a pink acrylic base with a 13 mm wide, 7 mm deep channel underneath (2 mm inner flange, 4 mm rolled outer border) and a row of white teeth on top. It lies teeth up on a paper towel on the bedside table, its front toward the arms and 15 mm over the table's edge. The table top (11.5 x 19 cm) is 17 cm up, its front edge 24.5 cm forward, and the denture is centred 12 cm right of the centre line; an empty denture cup stands beside it. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: 1.0 as soon as all of these hold, with the denture still, for 1 s: the denture seated on the lower ridge (centred within 2.5 mm, its channel within 2 mm of sitting on the ridge, turned under 5 degrees, tilted under 4 degrees, so it sits flat all round and does not rock when its front teeth are pressed), and each gripper's fingertip centre at least 3 cm in front of her lips. Otherwise, judged at the end of the run: 0.75: seated, but a gripper still at the mouth; 0.5: on the ridge but not seated (within 8 mm and tilted under 15 degrees, e.g. cocked on the crest); 0.25: in the mouth but not on the ridge; 0.0: still outside the mouth, or dropped. In a real trial, seating is checked by eye and by pressing the front teeth (no rock), with a ruler on the midline.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Lift the denture out of the mouth by its front teeth, lay it back on the paper towel as in the screenshot, and check the lower lip has sprung back.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1 with PhysX, 20 Hz control). Simplified: the head is boxes and spheres; gums, tongue and lips are rigid except the lower lip, a sprung flap; the denture is rigid, its channel 2.5 mm wider than the ridge on each side, where real soft tissue gives; saliva, suction and the resident's own movement are not modelled; cameras render at 320 x 176.
